analysis.one_liner: Bans big meatpackers from owning or feeding the livestock they slaughter.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Agriculture Committee: it was referred there on the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee, and died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change a 1921 law that governs meatpackers so that big packing companies could no longer own, feed, or control the cattle, hogs, or other livestock they buy for slaughter — unless the farmer running the operation still has a real say in managing it. The point is to stop the largest meat companies from vertically integrating: raising the animals themselves or locking farmers into contracts where the company controls everything. The bill never went anywhere; it was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and then a subcommittee, and it died there when the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent farmers and ranchers who raise livestock. If packers cannot own or control the animals themselves, independent producers have more customers bidding for their cattle and hogs and more bargaining power over contract terms. Rural communities that depend on farm income also stand to gain, and consumers could benefit from more competition among buyers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful for a packer to own, feed, or control livestock directly, through a subsidiary, or through any arrangement giving the packer operational, managerial, or supervisory control over the animals or the farm operation, where the farmer no longer materially participates in management [S3].
It closes a loophole the bill targets: packers raising animals through subsidiaries or contract arrangements that leave the farmer with the risk but not the control [S3].
Transition rules give swine packers 18 months and other packers up to 180 days to unwind existing ownership arrangements, so the ban does not wipe out existing arrangements overnight [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest meatpacking companies, which would have to divest the livestock they own or control and buy animals on the open market from independent producers. Some economists and packers argue that restricting packer-owned livestock raises costs and meat prices for consumers.

drawbacks.text: The bill contains broad carve-outs: animals held within 7 days of slaughter are exempt, farmer-owned cooperatives are exempt, small packers not required to report daily prices are exempt, and any packer that owns only one processing plant is exempt [S3].

Critics of packer-ownership bans generally argue that when companies like the big four packers lose the ability to secure their own supply, they may shift to long-term marketing contracts that give farmers little more bargaining power than before, and that processing costs could rise and be passed to consumers. This objection is not in the provided record; it is general knowledge about how the industry operates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For independent livestock producers, the potential gain is real: fewer packer-owned animals means more demand for what they raise. But the design is leaky — the one-plant exemption, the cooperative carve-out, and the 7-day rule each let a slice of packer ownership continue, and a packer could restructure into a one-plant subsidiary to escape the ban entirely. Whether consumers benefit depends on whether packers actually bid more at open market rather than shifting to contracts.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, then to its Livestock and Horticulture Subcommittee, and the Committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Leonard Boswell, an Iowa Democrat, introduced the bill on February 12, 2003, joined by original cosponsors from Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Nebraska — a largely farm-state, bipartisan group [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the same day, and on February 20 to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture [S5].
On February 24, 2003, the committee requested an executive comment from the U.S. Department of Agriculture [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the bill died in committee when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies that own and feed livestock are better off, because the ban never became law and they kept their existing supply arrangements. The House Agriculture Committee's inaction ended the bill despite bipartisan sponsorship from a dozen House members.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big meatpackers kept their supply arrangements

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was a Democrat and six of its eleven cosponsors were Republicans, all largely from Midwest farm states; the record shows no votes, so the partisan shape of any floor fight is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would bar packers from owning, feeding, or controlling the livestock they slaughter, forcing the largest companies to buy from independent producers on the open market. Their gain from the bill's death is independent farmers' loss of a potential bidding floor.
Farmers and ranchers who raise livestock would face packers bidding in an open market instead of supplying themselves, strengthening their bargaining position.
Cooperatives majority-owned by active members who supply their own livestock are exempted from the ban, so they could keep owning and feeding livestock for slaughter.
Packers that own only one plant or that do not have to report daily purchase prices are exempt, shielding smaller processors from the ban while it targets the biggest firms.
